doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Choosing and auditioning for Fredonia
summary: After failed or unappealing New York auditions he is drawn to Fredonia, aces the Bach audition, and is warned about few black students.

venues.name: High School of Music and Art

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I was going to ask how you ended up there.

Okay, what happened was that I had taken auditions for different schools. I tried Eastman, which I totally messed up. And Manhattan School of Music for some reason I took the theory, to be a theory major. And a student named David Butler had come down to the Music and Art and had talked up Fredonia. So there were about six of us from Music and Art, decided we’d look it up, you know, see what’s up. So I had gotten my teacher because she never was really hot on like Bach. And somehow I felt like I needed to learn this composer, for some reason. I said I’d like to learn some Bach. And so we got into the inventions first and then the fugues. So here I am at the audition for Fredonia and I kind of aced everything, right. And see Bach, although I wanted to do it, I wasn’t really comfortable with Bach you know. So I played everything thinking that would be it. And all of a sudden he says, “Do you know any Bach?” I said ahhh, why’d he ask me that question you know. Well I said okay I’ll do my C minor fugue. And I just breezed through it. And what happened, at that point he started telling me about the school. Now I © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

had already failed Eastman, I wasn’t too happy about New York College of Music and Manhattan School of Music because I felt I’d see myself at the clubs all night with a midterm the next day. Because I’d probably be at the clubs watching Milt Jackson or Herbie, instead of studying for an exam. So I said I need to get out of New York. So I finished the audition and he says, “Well Allan, you know there aren’t many black people in Fredonia.” My thing was I really don’t care, I want to know did I pass the audition or not.

He said that, he said that. I’ll never forget. Because he felt it would make a difference. Because here I am in the big city of Harlem — not a big city of Harlem — big city of New York, and I’m going to essentially a country town. You know I’ll never forget because downtown Fredonia reminded me of a scene from “In the Heat of the Night.” You know, just the opening scene of “In the Heat of the Night.” You’d go downtown, if you ever see it, it looks like downtown Fredonia. Okay? So anyway but at that point that was the farthest from my mind. So I decided to say listen did I make it? You know I don’t care about, you know. And he said yes. So I was happy. And of course the other five students also came to Fredonia so I felt good because the culture shock wasn’t that great, because actually my first roommate was Warren Hargut, who was from Music and Art. So it was really cool. And he ended up being one of my last roommates, when we shared—
